subtopics.name: Aging process and older adult health

questions.stem: On a busy medical unit, the nurse is caring for four clients, each with a different confirmed infection, and moves between their rooms through the shift. For each task, indicate the protective equipment and hand hygiene the nurse needs.

rows.text: Changing the dressing on a MRSA-infected leg wound
Giving oral medications to a client with influenza
Suctioning a ventilated client with COVID-19
Emptying the commode of a client with Clostridioides difficile

columns.text: Gown and gloves, alcohol hand rub
Surgical mask, eye protection and gloves
N95, eye protection, gown and gloves
Gown and gloves, then soap-and-water handwashing

rationale.correct: Match PPE and hand hygiene to how each organism spreads: contact (gown, gloves), droplet (mask, eye protection), aerosol-generating procedures (N95) and spores (soap and water).

perOption.r1:c1: Contact precautions with alcohol rub are correct for MRSA.
perOption.r1:c2: A mask is not the main need.
perOption.r1:c4: Soap and water are not required for MRSA.
perOption.r2:c2: Droplet precautions: surgical mask, with eye protection for close care.
perOption.r2:c3: An N95 is for aerosol-generating procedures or airborne diseases.
perOption.r3:c1: Not enough for an aerosol-generating procedure.
perOption.r3:c2: A surgical mask is not enough during aerosol-generating procedures.
perOption.r3:c3: Aerosol-generating procedures need an N95, eye protection, gown and gloves.
perOption.r4:c1: Alcohol does not kill C. difficile spores.
perOption.r4:c2: A mask is not the main need.
perOption.r4:c4: Contact precautions plus soap-and-water handwashing remove spores.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose PPE and hand hygiene by organism.

questions.stem: A client with a tunneled central venous catheter for chemotherapy has a temperature of 38.7 °C (101.7 °F) and chills that started during a line flush. The exit site is red with a small amount of pus. What should the nurse expect first?

options.text: Remove the catheter at the bedside right away and send the tip for culture
Blood cultures from the catheter and a peripheral vein, then IV antibiotics
A dose of acetaminophen and a recheck of the temperature in 4 hours
Flushing the line with heparin to clear any clot that may be causing the fever

rationale.correct: Suspected central line infection: paired blood cultures (line and peripheral), prompt antibiotics and provider evaluation of the line.

perOption.a: Tunneled catheters are removed by the provider if indicated; cultures and antibiotics come first.
perOption.b: Paired cultures help confirm a line infection, and antibiotics should start promptly.
perOption.c: Treating the fever alone delays treatment of a possible bloodstream infection.
perOption.d: Flushing an infected line can push organisms into the blood.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a suspected central line infection.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to enter the room of a client on contact and droplet precautions. Place the steps for putting on PPE in order.

items.text: Put on gloves, pulling them over the gown cuffs
Put on goggles or a face shield

rationale.correct: Donning order: hand hygiene, gown, mask or respirator, eye protection, gloves.

perOption.b: The gown goes on first so the gloves can cover its cuffs.
perOption.c: The mask goes on before eye protection.
perOption.d: Eye protection fits over the mask.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client and caregiver about caring for a permanent tracheostomy at home. Which instructions help prevent infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clean the hands before touching the tracheostomy
Clean the inner cannula as instructed, using clean technique
Rinse the inner cannula with tap water and put it back while wet
Keep the stoma covered with a breathable cover when outdoors
Share suction catheters between family members who need them

rationale.correct: Home tracheostomy care: hand hygiene, clean technique, proper cannula cleaning and a stoma cover outdoors.

perOption.a: Hand hygiene prevents carrying organisms into the airway.
perOption.b: Clean technique is used at home.
perOption.c: The cannula is rinsed with sterile or boiled water as instructed and dried.
perOption.d: Covers filter dust and cold air.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.stem: After a client fell at 0300, the team holds a post-fall huddle. Highlight the factors that most likely contributed to the fall.

segments.text: was walking to the bathroom alone in socks without grips
The call light was within reach
The bed alarm was turned off after the evening bath

rationale.correct: Post-fall reviews look for contributing factors such as sedatives, unassisted toileting, footwear and disabled alarms, to prevent the next fall.

perOption.s2: Sedative-hypnotics cause unsteadiness and confusion at night.
perOption.s4: Unassisted toileting and slippery socks are common contributors.
perOption.s6: This was in place and did not contribute.
perOption.s8: A disabled alarm removed a safety layer.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze factors in a client fall.

questions.stem: During a home visit, the nurse learns that an 81-year-old client fills prescriptions at three different pharmacies and sees four providers. What is the main safety concern?

options.text: The client may be spending more money than necessary on the same medications
No single pharmacist can check the client's drugs for interactions
The client may have trouble remembering which pharmacy holds each prescription
The client may run out of pills because refills come at different times

rationale.correct: Encourage one pharmacy and a complete medication list shared with every provider to prevent interactions and duplicates.

perOption.a: Cost matters, but it is not the main safety risk.
perOption.b: Using several pharmacies prevents a complete medication check, raising the risk of interactions and duplication.
perOption.c: This is an inconvenience but not the main risk.
perOption.d: Timing is less important than unrecognized interactions.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Identify a medication safety risk at home.

questions.stem: After a chemical release at a train yard, several workers who were near a leaking tank car arrive with pinpoint pupils, drooling, sweating, vomiting, wheezing and muscle twitching. They have already been decontaminated. Which treatment should the nurse prepare?

options.text: IV naloxone, because pinpoint pupils suggest opioid exposure
Atropine and pralidoxime as prescribed, given promptly
Calcium gluconate gel applied to the skin
Sodium thiosulfate and hydroxocobalamin for cyanide

rationale.correct: Nerve agent and organophosphate exposure causes cholinergic excess (SLUDGE and miosis); treat with atropine, pralidoxime and benzodiazepines for seizures.

perOption.a: Drooling, sweating, wheezing and twitching point to a cholinergic nerve agent or organophosphate, not opioids.
perOption.b: These signs show cholinergic excess from a nerve agent or organophosphate; atropine dries secretions and pralidoxime restores enzyme function.
perOption.c: Calcium gluconate is for hydrofluoric acid exposure.
perOption.d: Cyanide causes rapid collapse and acidosis, not this cholinergic picture.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: The nurse collects a blood specimen at the bedside. Which 2 identifiers must be on the specimen label, applied in front of the client?

options.text: The client's full name
The client's date of birth or medical record number
The client's room number
The client's admitting diagnosis
The client's bed position by the window

rationale.correct: Specimens are labeled at the bedside with two identifiers, such as name and date of birth or record number; never room numbers.

perOption.a: Name is one of the two identifiers.
perOption.b: A second unique identifier is required.

questions.stem: A client at 32 weeks of gestation comes for a prenatal visit. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or should be reported.

rows.text: Blood pressure 148/96 mm Hg, up from 112/70
Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Headache that will not go away and seeing spots
Irregular, painless tightening that eases with rest

rationale.correct: At 32 weeks, fundal height near 32 cm, mild ankle edema and Braxton Hicks are expected; new hypertension, persistent headache and visual changes need reporting.

perOption.r1:c1: Fundal height in cm roughly matches weeks between 20 and 36.
perOption.r2:c1: New hypertension after 20 weeks may be preeclampsia.
perOption.r3:c2: This is expected if no other signs.
perOption.r4:c1: These can be signs of severe preeclampsia.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish expected from concerning prenatal findings.

questions.stem: A first-time parent of a healthy 2-month-old who weighed 3.4 kg (7.5 lb) at birth asks the nurse how fast the baby should grow and when to switch from formula. Complete the sentences.

content.template: Most infants double their birth weight by about {{b1}} and triple it by {{b2}}. Cow's milk should not replace breast milk or formula until about {{b3}}.

options.text: 5 to 6 months
2 months
12 months
12 months
6 months
24 months
12 months
4 months
6 months

rationale.correct: Infants double birth weight by 5 to 6 months and triple it by 12 months; whole cow's milk is started at about 12 months.

perOption.b1:a: Birth weight usually doubles by 5 to 6 months.
perOption.b2:a: Birth weight usually triples by 1 year.
perOption.b2:c: Weight has more than tripled by then.
perOption.b3:a: Whole cow's milk is introduced at about 1 year.
perOption.b3:b: Cow's milk before 1 year can cause iron deficiency and kidney strain.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.educationalObjective: Apply infant growth and feeding milestones.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client who had chickenpox as a child asks about the shingles vaccine. The client had a single dose of the older live zoster vaccine 6 years ago. What should the nurse explain?

options.text: No further shingles vaccine is needed after the older live vaccine
Two doses of the recombinant zoster vaccine, starting at this visit
The vaccine is given once a person is over 65 years of age
The vaccine should wait until the client has an outbreak of shingles

rationale.correct: Recombinant zoster vaccine: two doses, 2 to 6 months apart, for adults 50 and older, including those who had the live vaccine or shingles before.

perOption.a: People who received the older live vaccine are advised to get the recombinant vaccine.
perOption.b: Adults 50 and older, including those who had the older vaccine, should receive two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine.
perOption.d: The vaccine is given to prevent shingles.

references: CDC/ACIP immunization schedules
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A sexually active 23-year-old client with a cervix and no symptoms has a routine visit. Which screenings should the nurse expect to be offered? Select all that apply.

options.text: Chlamydia and gonorrhea testing
HIV testing at least once
Cervical cytology if not done in the last 3 years
A screening colonoscopy for colorectal cancer
Blood pressure measurement
A screening mammogram for breast cancer

rationale.correct: Young adults: chlamydia and gonorrhea screening under 25 (cervix), HIV at least once, cervical cytology every 3 years from 21 and blood pressure.

perOption.a: Recommended yearly for sexually active people with a cervix under 25.
perOption.d: Colorectal screening starts at 45 for average risk.
perOption.f: Not recommended at this age for average risk.

references: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations
CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.educationalObjective: Plan screening for a young adult.

questions.stem: A client starting medroxyprogesterone acetate injections for contraception asks about the plan. Which statement shows understanding?

options.text: "I'll get a shot once a month, on the same day each month."
"I'll get a shot every 12 to 13 weeks and protect my bones."
"My periods will stay completely regular each month while I'm on the shot."
"I'll be fertile again within a week of my last shot."

rationale.correct: Medroxyprogesterone injection: every 12 to 13 weeks, irregular bleeding is common, fertility may be delayed and bone density may decrease.

perOption.a: The injection is given every 12 to 13 weeks.
perOption.b: Injections are every 3 months, and the drug can lower bone density, so bone health measures are advised.
perOption.c: Irregular bleeding or no periods are common.
perOption.d: Return of fertility can take 10 months or longer.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)

questions.stem: For each child, choose the type of play most typical for their age.

options.text: Solitary play with toys within reach
Cooperative games with rules
Parallel play beside other children
Cooperative team sports
Parallel play beside other children
Board games with strict rules
Associative play, sharing toys loosely in a group
Solitary play only
Organized competitive leagues
Parallel play
Associative play
Cooperative play with rules and roles

rationale.correct: Play develops from solitary (infant) to parallel (toddler), associative (preschool) and cooperative play with rules (school age).

perOption.b2:b: Toddlers play next to, not with, others.
perOption.b3:a: Preschoolers play together without fixed roles.
perOption.b4:c: School-age children play organized games with rules.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: On the third day after a vaginal birth, a client's lochia had become pinkish-brown. Today it is heavy and bright red again, with clots. The fundus is firm at the umbilicus. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: A normal return to lochia rubra after more activity at home
Retained placental fragments or subinvolution
The start of the client's first menstrual period after birth
Expected lochia serosa, which is often red with clots

rationale.correct: Lochia moves from rubra to serosa to alba; a return to bright red bleeding with clots suggests retained fragments or subinvolution and needs evaluation.

perOption.a: A return to heavy bright red bleeding after it has lightened is not normal.
perOption.b: Bleeding that returns to bright red with clots suggests retained tissue or delayed involution, even if the fundus feels firm.
perOption.c: Menstruation does not return this early.
perOption.d: Lochia serosa is pinkish-brown, not bright red with clots.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: At a 12-month well-child visit, the parent says the family lives in a house built in 1950 that is being renovated, and the child often chews on windowsills. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Recommend washing the child's hands before meals and recheck at 2 years
Arrange a blood lead test now and teach ways to limit exposure
Suggest an iron supplement to prevent anemia from the paint
Tell the parent that lead is a risk in homes built after 1978, not before

rationale.correct: Children in housing built before 1978, especially during renovation, need blood lead testing at 12 and 24 months and exposure reduction.

perOption.a: Hand washing helps but does not replace testing a child at high risk.
perOption.b: Older homes, renovation and chewing on painted surfaces put the child at high risk; testing now guides care.
perOption.c: Iron does not treat lead exposure, though good nutrition helps.
perOption.d: Lead paint was used before 1978, so older homes are the risk.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old client with no symptoms has an annual wellness visit and returns to review the results of screening tests. Highlight the results that need follow-up.

rationale.correct: Follow up high LDL, elevated blood pressure and any positive stool-based colorectal screen with colonoscopy.

perOption.r1: Very high LDL needs treatment planning.
perOption.r5: A positive FIT needs a follow-up colonoscopy.

questions.stem: A client who has taken alprazolam 2 mg three times daily for 5 years ran out 3 days ago. The client now has severe anxiety, tremor, sweating, insomnia, heart rate 118/min, blood pressure 162/98 mm Hg and says the room "looks like it's moving." Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Notify the provider to restart a benzodiazepine and plan a slow taper
Encourage the client to manage without medication from now on
Give flumazenil to reverse the symptoms
Offer coffee to help the client feel more alert

rationale.correct: Long-term benzodiazepines must be tapered; abrupt stopping can cause severe withdrawal and seizures. Restart and taper, use seizure precautions and monitor vital signs.

perOption.c1: Stopping a long-term benzodiazepine suddenly causes anxiety, tremor, autonomic overactivity and perceptual changes, with a risk of seizures.
perOption.c2: Anxiety alone does not cause tremor, autonomic instability and perceptual changes days after stopping a benzodiazepine.
perOption.c3: The timing after stopping alprazolam points to withdrawal.
perOption.c4: The client was taking a benzodiazepine, not an opioid.
perOption.a1: A controlled taper prevents seizures and severe withdrawal.
perOption.a4: Flumazenil would worsen withdrawal and can cause seizures.
perOption.p1: Show the severity of withdrawal and response to treatment.
perOption.p2: Seizures are the most dangerous complication.
perOption.p3: Not relevant to the acute withdrawal.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: On an inpatient unit, the nurse notes how four different clients are coping with stress during their stay. For each statement or behavior, indicate the defense mechanism it shows.

rows.text: A client angry at the provider yells at the dietary aide about cold food
A client who dislikes a roommate says, "That roommate hates me."
A grieving client channels sadness into running a fundraiser
A 30-year-old hospitalized client curls up and sucks their thumb

rationale.correct: Projection: attributing own feelings to others. Displacement: redirecting feelings to a safer target. Sublimation: channeling into constructive action. Regression: returning to earlier behavior.

perOption.r1:c1: The client is not blaming others for their own feelings.
perOption.r1:c2: Anger is moved to a safer target.
perOption.r1:c3: This is not a healthy outlet.
perOption.r1:c4: The client is not returning to childlike behavior.
perOption.r2:c1: The client attributes their own feeling to someone else.
perOption.r3:c3: Turning distress into constructive action is sublimation.
perOption.r4:c4: Returning to earlier behavior under stress is regression.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with bipolar disorder in a manic episode says, "I'm the president of a secret world bank and I'm buying this hospital tomorrow." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "That's not true. You're not the president of any bank."
"You feel very important right now. How have you been sleeping?"
"Tell me more about your plans to buy the hospital."
"If you were the president, you wouldn't be in the hospital."

rationale.correct: With grandiose delusions, do not argue or reinforce; acknowledge the underlying feeling and redirect to reality.

perOption.a: Arguing with a delusion increases agitation.
perOption.b: Acknowledging the feeling without agreeing and redirecting to reality-based concerns is therapeutic.
perOption.c: Asking for details reinforces the delusion.
perOption.d: Logical arguments do not change delusions and can increase agitation.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with major depression is admitted after a suicide attempt and says they still want to die. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continuous one-to-one observation
Removing belts, shoelaces and sharp objects from the room
Asking the client to sign a no-suicide contract instead of observation
Checking belongings and items brought by visitors
Asking directly and regularly about suicidal thoughts
Placing the client in the room farthest from the nurses' station

rationale.correct: High suicide risk: continuous observation, remove means, check belongings, assess regularly and keep the client near staff; no-suicide contracts are not protective.

perOption.c: Contracts do not prevent suicide and do not replace observation.
perOption.f: Clients at risk should be close to staff.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care for a client at high suicide risk.

questions.stem: A nurse volunteers at a shelter the day after a flood destroyed many homes. A resident is tearful, says they cannot think straight and has not eaten. Which action reflects psychological first aid?

options.text: Ask the resident to describe the flood in detail to work through the trauma
Meet basic needs such as food and rest and link the resident to support
Diagnose the resident with PTSD and start counseling sessions right away
Tell the resident to stay strong for the sake of their family

rationale.correct: Psychological first aid: promote safety, calm, basic needs, connection and hope; avoid forcing people to retell trauma.

perOption.a: Pushing for detailed accounts can increase distress; debriefing is not recommended early.
perOption.b: Psychological first aid focuses on safety, basic needs, calm and connection to support.
perOption.c: PTSD cannot be diagnosed the day after a trauma.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the family of a client with opioid use disorder how to use a naloxone nasal spray. Which statement by a family member shows understanding?

options.text: "I'll give the spray and then let them sleep it off on the couch at home."
"I'll call 911, give the spray, and repeat it if there's no response."
"I'll use the spray once they have stopped breathing completely."
"I'll keep the spray in the refrigerator so it lasts longer."

rationale.correct: For suspected opioid overdose: call 911, give naloxone, start rescue breathing or CPR if needed, repeat doses every 2 to 3 minutes and stay until help arrives.

perOption.a: Naloxone wears off; the person needs emergency care and monitoring.
perOption.b: Calling for help, giving naloxone and repeating if needed is the correct response.
perOption.c: Give naloxone for suspected overdose with unresponsiveness or slow breathing.
perOption.d: Naloxone is stored at room temperature and should be easy to reach.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: Place the phases of the nurse-client relationship in the order they occur.

items.text: Working: the client explores problems and practices new behaviors
Termination: the nurse and client review progress and say goodbye
Orientation: the nurse and client establish trust and the contract
Preorientation: the nurse reviews data and examines their own feelings

rationale.correct: Peplau's phases: preorientation, orientation, working and termination.
references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)

questions.stem: A client with bulimia nervosa finishes lunch on an eating disorder unit and immediately asks to use the bathroom. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Allow the client to go alone, since privacy builds trust in the relationship
Ask the client to stay with staff in the common area for 1 to 2 hours
Tell the client that bathrooms are locked for the whole day
Give the client a laxative so they do not need to purge

rationale.correct: On eating disorder units, clients are supervised for 1 to 2 hours after meals to prevent purging.

perOption.a: The client may purge after a meal.
perOption.c: Complete restriction is not necessary or humane.
perOption.d: Laxatives are a form of purging.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
